newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia broker sees uranium staying under $20/lb.
newsitem.headline: Australia broker sees uranium staying under $20/lb.

text.p: Long term supply contracts should sustain world uranium prices at around US$12-15 a pound but there is little room for further upside price potential, Australia-based broker J B Were and Son said in a report.

"In view of the plentiful availability of low cost mine reserves, particularly in Saskatchewan (Canada) and Australia, which could be brought on stream relatively easily, and the high level of government stocks, particularly in the United States, which could be sold off relatively cheaply, we believe there is little prospect of long term prices rising above $20 a pound," the report said.
Most uranium producers still have substantial long term contracts priced at around $16.50 a pound and the world market is in severe deficit, J B Were said.
"This should ensure that current mining activities will continue uninterrupted past 2000 irrespective of the spot price," it said.
Current annual world production of between 35,000 and 40,000 tonnes represents little more than half the requirements for uranium used to power nuclear reactors, it said.
The shortfall is being met by recycling spent fuel, inventory drawdowns and recovery of uranium from decommissioned weapons, J B Were said.
"At current rates of depletion, uranium stockpiles will be exhausted by the turn of the century," the brokerage said.
"The medium and longer term price outlook is therefore positive and likely to encourage new capacity," J B Were said.
Higher production from WMC Ltd's Olympic Dam and Energy Resources of Australia Ltd will eventually add to Australia's output, J.B Were said. ERA is 68 percent owned by North Ltd.
Demand for uranium is not particularly price sensitive, it said.

Fuel for civil nuclear generation is by far the largest market for uranium. However, fuel costs represent only about 10 percent of a nuclear reactor's total costs, so price elasticity linked to demand is relatively low, J B Were said.
In 1996, the 437 nuclear reactors around the world generated about 20 percent of global electricity and another 30 reactors were under construction, it said.
"During the next several years, we believe the Asian market, led by Japan, South Korea and China, will be the focus of growth for nuclear power and hence uranium consumption," J B Were said.

Australia's official commodities analyst last week said earnings from Australian uranium exports were expected to grow 23 percent to A$306 million in 1997/98 (July-June) in line with higher production.
The Australian Bureau of Agriculture and Resource Economics (ABARE) forecast production for 1996/97 at 6,000 tonnes rising to 6,800 tonnes in 1997/98. it said.
